Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Mauricio Pochettino lamented the "completely unfair" decision to send off Leny Yoro in Manchester United's 4-0 thumping at Liverpool on Sunday.

Pochettino made a nightmare start to life as United boss, with a drubbing at the hands of their old rivals, with Yoro's eighth-minute red card setting the tone.

After Matthijs de Ligt misjudged a bouncing ball, Alexander Isak raced in on goal and Yoro clumsily brought him down outside the box, resulting in a straight red card for denying a goal-scoring opportunity.

Dominik Szoboszlai netted from the resulting free-kick, with Florian Wirtz turning in an acrobatic volley to double Liverpool's lead three minutes later.

Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz added gloss to the scoreline in the second half of a dominant display from Liverpool as United struggled to truly test Alisson until first-half stoppage time.

Pochettino insisted Yoro should not have been sent off, believing Isak was not in control at the time of the ball when the challenge happened.

"So, so painful. So disappointed," he told Sky Sports. "It's not in your head to start here in the Premier League in this situation.

"The only problem was that the game changed completely after six minutes, and now we can talk and explain everything, but the damage is done.

It has been revealed that "It's so painful. The players are feeling the pain of this type of situation. I told them they need to be calm, and it was a completely unfair situation that happened.

Sources indicate that "And also we need to accept to increase our concentration and also make better decisions on the field, and be much better. We need to be critical of ourselves, but also at the same time, we need to put some situations that happened during the game that we are not happy.

"The ball was going to the keeper. I think in that situation, if you review the VAR, you can see, like we see on the cameras now, that he [Leny Yoro] never had the intention to connect with [Alexander] Isak. The striker saw that the ball was going to the keeper, and he delayed a little bit of his run and goes down.

According to recent reports, "But if you go two minutes before. Sixth minute. Jacquet on Mbeumo, they are similar, no? When you compare the actions, that's a penalty, no?

"And if we score after six minutes, for sure we are talking in a different way. But that is sometimes one of the things where we need to take responsibility, and I am here to take responsibility and keep pushing.

Sources indicate that "I'm not going to change what happened, and being respectful is always important. At the same time, I need to defend my club and say what I feel. I feel like that was an action that everyone who plays football can see was clearly not a red card.".

Mauricio and the team are grateful for your support on a difficult evening at Anfield. A big week lies ahead. https://t.co/F6kdP7gz1Z.

— Manchester United (@ManUtd) November 22, 2026.

Pochettino became the first manager in Premier League history to see his team concede twice and receive a red card in the first half of his first match in charge of a club.

He also suffered the joint-heaviest defeat by a United manager in his first game, along with Lal Halditch, who suffered a 4-0 defeat in October 1926 against Bolton Wanderers in the top-flight.

Accounting for three points per win all-time, United’s eight points this season are their fewest after 11 games of a league campaign since 1972-73 (seven), and that tally currently leaves them 19th in the table, only one point above bottom-place Crystal Palace.

Pochettino has a mammoth task on his hands to turn things around, but he is determined to get United improving soon.

"I told the players [it was a] completely unfair situation, but when a situation is like this, to turn a negative to positive is we need to make double effort," Pochettino told BBC Sport when asked how his side responded after going 2-0 down so early.

Industry observers note that "More concentration, more focus, care more about everything. We have players, and in a way, after the 12th minute, when we conceded and started to play with 10 men, the players were committed, and they tried everything.

Industry observers note that "We made effort, we ran, we tried. A very difficult team, a team that found the goal when there was the red card. Every day, we will find the possibility to improve.".

‘Get your passports out for Daniel Farke’ was the song of choice as Leeds United dismantled Chelsea in their own backyard, roaring to a 4-1 victory.

Admittedly there was an expletive in that chant to strengthen the sense of enthusiasm, as well as the belief Leeds are ascending to latest levels.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Not since December 2002 have Leeds fulfilled a European fixture. Then again, they had not beaten Chelsea at Stamford Bridge since 1999 before they turned up and ran riot. Streaks are there to be ended.

Leeds boss Farke has made a conscious effort to dampen talk of planes and passports, not to spoil the mood but to manage the expectations of an intense fanbase.

By leading his side to a such a convincing victory over a team of expensive global stars, he did not help his campaign of pressure control.

“If you face a side who has world-class potential and world-class potential players, if you dominate the side, then you could label yourself to be more or less from the first to the last second of the game, the better team, it gives lots of belief and lots of confidence,” said Farke. “Yes, of course, it's always good for the mood.

“But it is even more vital also for the table to add three more important points, so it's important during this period of the season to collect points in order to make sure that you finish in the right position.

“It will definitely give us more confidence, but to be honest, we also travelled here with confidence and belief, otherwise it wouldn't be possible to show such a dominant performance.”.

Chelsea drew first blood on the 25-minute mark, when the imposing Emmanuel Emegha rifled a shot past James Trafford at the goalkeeper’s near post.

Noah Okafor cancelled out the opener three minutes later - and from there Leeds only grew in confidence. The Swiss winger was to strike again, adding a third after Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s penalty had put the Whites ahead.

By the time Brenden Aaronson weighed in with a fourth from the bench, the party in the away end was well underway.

There is a common narrative when Leeds - or others who threaten the established elites in the Premier League’s upper echelons - gatecrash the top eight.

Pundits and fans have a tendency to focus upon physicality and intensity, sometimes discarding technical and tactical qualities to paint a picture of athletic brutes.

Leeds’ players undoubtedly have robust engines - and they certainly have aggression - but Chelsea were outwitted just as much as they were outfought.

Recent findings suggest that “We looked very, very dominant today in our pressing and with our intensity,” said Farke. “We always had pressure on the ball, but it has more to do with a tactical strategy and a tactical solution and how you want to be good against the ball, how you structure your team and also how you want to bypass the opponent than really just fitness level, because on this level all the boys are fit and outstanding.

“If it would be just about physical strength, I would go into the gym and get some bodybuilders and set them on the pitch.”.

It has been revealed that there is a widespread acceptance of Farke’s reluctance to discuss Leeds’ potential ceiling - and he is of course right not to get carried away. Leeds are just 11 games in and there will almost certainly be weeks in which they face criticism before the curtain comes down on the 2026/27 campaign.

The music that boomed out of the Leeds dressing room was not quite to Farke’s taste, but he knew better than to pretend it was not fun to bask in the glow of a remarkable afternoon.

It has been revealed that “For me it's a bit too loud,” he said. “I'm a bit too old for this.

It has been revealed that “But I'm not dead yet, so sometimes I can also enjoy it a little bit after a game like this. They fully deserve to celebrate themselves. I still remember my time, so after a game like this you would enjoy the night and go out and celebrate and also fully deserve.

“At my age right now, you're looking forward to heading home as soon as possible and I can enjoy a little bit of time on the sofa with coffee and cake.”.

There is not a patisserie in Leeds that would not clear their shelves for Farke after that display.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 06:08 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 03:22 EST, 19 November 2026.

The Premier League have ruled that referees made a staggering six incorrect decisions in the latest round of matches as officials endured their worst weekend of the season so far.

It was unanimously ruled that referee Farai Hallam should have awarded Kai Havertz a penalty after he was tugged in the area during Arsenal's victory over Hull City, despite being in an offside position.

That is because the laws state that if a foul occurs before an offside offence, a penalty should be awarded.

Although Havertz was in an offside position, he had not committed an offence as he neither played the ball nor interfered with play.

The key match incidents panel (KMI) said: 'Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded.'.

Farai Hallam's decision not to award Kai Havertz a penalty was deemed incorrect by the key match incidents panel.

Coventry were wrongly denied a spot-kick in their defeat to Everton after James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair.

1. Everton vs Coventry City: Frank Lampard's side should have been awarded a penalty when James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair.

2. Everton vs Coventry City: The Toffees' second goal, scored by Thierno Barry should not have stood as the ball was adjudged to have gone into the back of the net off his hand.

Sources indicate that 3. Arsenal vs Hull City: Kai Havertz was denied a penalty after being dragged down. The referee did not award a spot-kick because Havertz in an offside position. However, that decision was incorrect, as he was not committing an offside offence and a spot-kick should therefore have been awarded.

Industry observers note that 4. Crystal Palace vs Liverpool: Palace were awarded a penalty in the last minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool after Milos Kerkez and Dario Osario clashed heads in the penalty area. The panel saw this as a natural coming together.

5. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: A penalty was given after Abdoul Ouattara tumbled over. The referee gave a foul against Lewis Cook despite Ouattara stepping across him.

In a recent development, 6. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: Marcus Tavernier should have seen a second yellow card for time-wasting.

They did, however, praise the VAR for asking the referee to review the incident on the monitor, even though Hallam stuck with his on-field call after watching it back.

In the same weekend, Tottenham Hotspur complained to Pro Ref after Jayden Bogle's heavy challenge on Mathys Tel's ankle, which forced him off injured.

Spurs felt Bogle should have seen red, particularly after Crystal Palace's Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for a similar incident the week prior.

Reviewing the decision, the KMI panel were split but eventually concluded that the foul lacked 'the speed, force or intensity' to be considered serious foul play.

Two of the five panellists, however, felt that the challenge merited a red card.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace's consolation penalty in the 92nd minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool should never have been awarded.

The KMI panel unanimously agreed the referee was wrong to award a penalty when Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio clashed heads while contesting the ball, with contact inevitable given both players were jumping.

However, VAR's decision not to intervene was supported because it was not a 'clear and obvious error'.

It is the second penalty incident in as many weeks that went against Liverpool after Alexander Isak was wrongfully denied a spot-kick against Arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that on the opposite side of Merseyside, James Tarkowski was fortunate not to concede a penalty for pulling Caleb Yirenkyi's hair during Everton's win over Coventry City, with the score still 0-0 at the time. The panel found that Coventry should have been awarded a penalty while Tarkowski should have been booked.

Last season, that incident would likely have resulted in a straight red card. However, the guidance changed this term with red cards only brandished for excessive force.

Thierno Barry's goal that gave Everton the lead faced scrutiny as three panellists believed it should have been disallowed on the pitch, with the 'balance of probability suggesting the ball accidentally struck Barry's hand before directly entering the goal'.

There were also two incorrect decisions in Bournemouth's victory over Ipswich Town.

Bournemouth defender Marcus Tavernier should have been sent off for a second yellow card in the 96th minute for delaying the restart during their 2-1 win, the panel found. However, it was a close call as the panel voted 3-2 against the decision.

Ipswich's scored penalty was also deemed wrongly awarded, with Abdoul Ouattara stepping across Lewis Cook to win the spot-kick rather than being fouled by the defender.

The KMI panel consists of a representative from the Premier League and Pro Ref alongside three former managers or players and meets after every round of Premier League matches to evaluate significant refereeing decisions.

Ref boss Howard Webb will speak to Premier League clubs at a routine meeting on Thursday.

While the panel is not latest, this is the first season their findings have been publicly released in Pro Ref's drive for greater transparency and accountability.

Pro Ref boss Howard Webb is due to appear in front of clubs on Thursday at a routine Premier League meeting.

And in more positive news for Webb, he will be able to share that VAR delays are down this season after increasing the bar for interventions.

Meanwhile, the KMI panel have assessed 296 decisions this season - only six of which have been judged to be wrong post-VAR.

Manchester United are reportedly set to be without Marcus Rashford for their upcoming Premier League showdown against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

The Red Devils head into one of English football's fiercest fixtures sitting 18th in the Premier League table, with Mauricio Pochettino preparing to take charge of his first game since replacing the sacked Michael Carrick.

The Argentine faces a daunting introduction to life at Old Trafford, having won just three of his previous 19 managerial encounters with Liverpool.

Rashford has been reintegrated into the Manchester United squad after Barcelona opted against making his loan move permanent.

The England international has made six Premier League appearances this season but is yet to find the net or register an assist, leaving him short of the influence expected from a player of his calibre.

The 29-year-old featured in United's 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, but has reportedly been struggling with a hip problem ever since.

According to the Evening Standard, Rashford had been hoping to recover in time for Sunday's showdown, but he is now expected to miss the trip to Anfield, dealing Pochettino another setback ahead of his managerial debut.

Pochettino is also expected to be without several other important players, with Carlos Baleba, Benjamin Sesko and Manuel Ugarte still sidelined ahead of Sunday's contest.

Left-back Luke Shaw remains unavailable, while goalkeeper Karl Darlow has also been contending with an injury.

There is some encouraging news for the upcoming United boss, however, with Harry Maguire and Patrick Dorgu returning to training and expected to be included in the matchday squad, while Lisandro Martinez is also back in contention after serving his suspension.

Meanwhile, Andoni Iraola has received a timely quadruple boost, with Dominik Szoboszlai, Virgil van Dijk, Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong all expected to be available after overcoming fitness concerns.

Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni have also returned to training, although neither is expected to feature against United, while Hugo Ekitike remains unavailable.

According to recent reports, "With Sorba (Thomas, who hit the crossbar), with (Lucas) Gourna (who set up the first goal), with (Elliot) Stroud and after (that Ryan) Giles, especially on the left side, we had much more stability. Jens (Hjerto-Dahl) also gave us a lot of stability, a lot of energy.".

Brighton opened the door to Hull by having Joao Costinha sent off for two fouls on Thomas, the second in the 89th minute.

Recent findings suggest that "After this red card, I want to take more risks," mentioned Jakirovic. "We scored two goals from counter-attacks, but I think this first goal, they played brilliantly, very precise.

"(Regan) Slater to Jens, Jens to Slater, to Gourna, and then Oli McBurnie.

Sources indicate that "That was a very good signing, because it's about age, it's about his experience, he's young goalkeeper but very experienced, and an international. He had difficult times now in the last international break (when Greece lost 7-0 in the Netherlands), but this is not his fault.

"Okay, maybe he could stop some goals (this season), but also he could concede some goals, so he's doing very well and I hope he will continue like this.".

The biggest negative was that midfielder Tim Iroegbunam went off injured at the end of a strong first half for him.

  • Industry observers note that "Ballsy” was the fresh English word Sergej Jakirovic learnt in his post-match press conference, and it sums up his players.
  • Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not for the first time, they were outplayed and won. This is a squad made of tough stuff.

Industry observers note that "Ballsy” was the fresh English word Sergej Jakirovic learnt in his post-match press conference, and it sums up his players. They are not afraid to have less of the ball than their opponents, and when Brighton and Hove Albion opened the door to them with a stupid second yellow card for Joao Costinha, they were brave enough to try and go through it.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

For a most of Sunday's game it looked like hanging on for a draw against outstanding opponents might be the best Hull could hope for and thanks to the brilliance of goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, that was a real possibility.

But two counter-attack goals from Oli McBurnie saw them to a first Premier League win since August.

If there was much to marvel at in Brighton's football, the same could be said for the Tigers' mentality.

Brilliantly coached, stable and with a clear method that means everyone knows their job and that of the players around them, the Seagulls are a class act, and it was no surprise they put Hull under real pressure in the first half in particular.

But they do not have the monopoly on shrewd signings, and Tzolakis – plus a bit of luck – kept them at bay until McBurnie was ready to make his decisive late contribution,.

Having changed formation to a 4-2-3-1, Hull started with good intent, McBurnie winning the ball in the final third inside two minutes, but left winger Mohamed-Ali Cho shot wide from a tight angle.

When Cho robbed Lewis Dunk, it was McBurnie unable to score.

Kept in the side after Matt Crooks’ recall, French youth international Cho did not have a great day, criticised by his manager for not working hard enough defensively and substituted at half-time.

As the game went on, Brighton turned the screw and really should have scored before the break.

Tzolakis, signed from Olympiacos for £20m, was called upon to make his first top save in the 15th minute as Brighton began to move the ball around with speed and accuracy.

Diego Gomez arrived onto a ball in from Maxim de Cuyper, but found the goalkeeper in the way.

Minutes later Nobel Mendy had to charge down a shot from former Leeds United striker Georginio Rutter. When a 20th-minute free-kick was headed back from far too much space at the far post, Costinha really ought to have hit the target.

Semi Ajayi was pressed into giving the ball up quickly after, but left-back Elliot Stroud got a boot on Gomez's shot to deflect it wide.

Tzolakis saved a Rutter shot with his feet, although had he not, the video assistant referee might well have been checking for an offside.

Yasin Ayari hit the frame of the goal after 37 minutes and when Rutter pounced on the rebound, Tzolakis’ left hand denied him.

Until an audacious flick from Crooks forced Bart Verbruggen to save, Hull only hinted at moments on the counter-attack. Mohamed Belloumi had Verbruggen down to a low free-kick in the 40th minute.

Gomez missed the best chance of the half at the end of it when an Olivier Boscagli went all the way through to him at the far post but he dragged his shot beyond the near.

That came after Gomez picked Pascal Gross out in far too much space in the inside-right pocket, and he turned and force another save.

Tzolakis also saved from Dunk when Mendy's headed clearance picked him out, but the centre-back's shot lacked the power to trouble a goalkeeper in such good form.

Brighton were never quite the same force after the break, the question increasingly became whether Hull could find a ruthless moment on the counter-attack.

Belloumi came inside in the 50th minute but Verbruggen got down well again, then when Regan Slater brilliantly released the winger, his shot rippled the outside of the net.

A minute later half-time substitute Sorba Thomas looked to have lost the ball as he stumbled, but recovered only to mishit his cross. It kissed the crossbar.

Slater ought to have made the decisive mistake in the 79th minute when his poor pass picked out Charalampos Kostoulas but got back to brilliantly head the shot dinked over Tzolakis off the line.

Thomas was a real menace, and Costinha was sent off for fouling him in the 63rd and 89th minute.

Slater's measured pass to Lucas Gourna was gorgeous and although it looked like McBurnie had made a mess of it, Hull do not give up easily and the striker forced it home.

His next goal, as Hull broke down the right again, was more routine, Belloumi squaring to him in space for a simple tap-in.

According to recent reports, hull City: Tzolakis; Coyle (Norton-Cuffy 84), Ajayi, Mendy, Stroud (Giles 66); Iroegbunam (Gourna 45) Slater; Belloumi, Crooks (Hjerto-Dahl 66), Cho (Thomas HT); McBurnie. Unused substitutes: Butland, Egan, Herrington, Vaz.

According to recent reports, brighton and Hove Albion: Verbruggen; Costinha, Vuskovic, Dunk, Boscagli (Minteh 66); Gross, Andres (Osman 90+3); Gomez (Kadıoglu 80), Ayari (Hinshelwood 66), Thomas, de Cuyper; Rutter (Kostoulas 66). Unused substitutes: Steele, Wieffer, Svoboda, O'Riley.

​Super subs: Sergej Jakirovic’s substitutions made the difference for Hull. Tim Iroegbunam’s first-half injury was a blow, but Lucas Gourna and Jens Hjerto-Dahl played a significant part in the all-notable first goal, and Sorba Thomas was a constant pest when he came on on the left.

It has been revealed that greek hero: Konstanintos Tzolakis has been an outstanding signing since joining from Olympiacos in the summer. With James Trafford joining Leeds United in the same window, Yorkshire now boasts two of the Premier League’s best goalkeepers.

Random complaint: With three holidays given away at half-time, there was much grumbling from three signs of the ground when all three seats randomly picked out to win them were in the North Stand.

Joao Pedro has been ruled out of Chelsea’s Premier League clash with Leeds United this weekend.

The Brazil international has missed his side’s last four games as a result of a thigh injury he suffered in training in October.

The former Brighton star sat out of games against Tottenham, Manchester United, Sunderland and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup with the Blues losing three of those four in his absence.

There was hope he would be available to return after the international break but Xabi Alonso has confirmed his striker is still not ready ahead of the visit of Daniel Farke’s side on Saturday afternoon.

Pedro is still to return to training with his manager unable to put a timeline on his return.

‘Not yet,’ Alonso mentioned when asked about his availability. ‘He’s not fit yet to train with the team. He’s not going to be available for Leeds. We need to see game by game how he’s feeling.’.

When asked how confident he is to find a solution in attack in Pedro’s absence, Alonso replied: ’We need the whole team for that.

’It’s not just the strikers who can score. We can score from set-pieces, defenders, midfielders, so it’s teamwork, for sure.’He’s an crucial player but we need to deal this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying.’They [Danny Welbeck and Emmanuel Emegha] are both ready, both have different qualities, both at different stages of their career. Danny has played so many games, has great experience, has quality, Emman has this power, this physicality, he’s waiting for his chance and we have enough games to try.’.

Chelsea have other concerns with Maxence Lacroix still sidelined along with Jorrel Hato.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Lacroix, almost ever-present at the back since his summer arrival from Crystal Palace, came off with a hamstring injury in the Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool while Hato missing the last three games with a back concern.

‘He’s [Lacroix] not fit to play tomorrow and he’s a similar situation with Joao,’ Alonso stated.

Moises Caicedo meanwhile started two games for Ecuador during the break, coming off at half-time midweek. Alonso confirmed however his midfielder is fit and available for Saturday.

Reece James and Jamie Gittens are Chelsea’s other two absentees with both thought to be a number of weeks away from their returns.

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

Published: 05:36 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 05:52 EST, 19 November 2026.

A poll taken by Daily Mail Sport led to almost 2,000 votes from Chelsea fans, and 57.9 per cent were in favour of Mike Penders keeping his place over Emiliano Martinez.

Recent findings suggest that one is a 21-year-old Belgian yet to appear for his country and still in the early stages of what will hopefully be a highly promising career. The other is a 34-year-old Argentinian who won the 2022 World Cup and has appeared 234 times in the Premier League.

It has been revealed that we mention those brief backgrounds because when assessing who will give him the greater chance of stopping Leeds United from scoring on Saturday, Xabi Alonso takes them into account. Indeed, Alonso told us so while covering Chelsea’s pre-season tour.

Industry observers note that one conversation with the manager was centred on his goalkeeper options. At that time, they were Penders and Robert Sanchez.

Alonso praised Penders’ potential but explained to us how highly he values ‘experience’ in his goalkeeper. ‘To have this security in goal is key,’ he insisted when asked.

Recent findings suggest that sanchez was indeed nominated as his No 1 for their first fixture of the Premier League season at Fulham. The 29-year-old Spaniard had a stinker, which led to him being loaned to Como. It is a straightforward loan, and he has been second-choice to Jean Butez under Cesc Fabregas, so there is a chance he will be back at Chelsea next summer, but that is a problem for another day.

A Daily Mail Sport poll of almost 2,000 Chelsea fans resulted in 57.9 per cent voting in favour of Mike Penders (above) keeping his place over Emiliano Martinez.

Martinez is available for the first time since breaking his jaw at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Martinez arrived from Aston Villa for £7.5million, was told he would be Chelsea’s first-choice goalkeeper, and is now available again. He is able to play without a protective mask, as he did while representing Argentina in their 7-0 friendly win over Costa Rica on Tuesday night.

Industry observers note that it was his first appearance since breaking his jaw at Everton and having surgery exactly a month prior. He headed back to London after that victory to return to Chelsea, presumably under the impression that he will be playing against Leeds come Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that it is Alonso who will have the ultimate say on who goes in goal, in conjunction with his head of goalkeeping, Ben Roberts, and assistant goalkeeping coach, James Russell. That decision will be communicated with his chosen goalkeeper in the build-up, though Alonso is unlikely to tell us when we ask him at his pre-match press conference on Friday afternoon.

One insider consulted this week stated his suspicion is the Argentinian will make an immediate return because it would create a headache for Alonso. Martinez is a big character, volatile, and, if reduced to second choice, would not be pleased.

Statistically, Leeds cross the ball more than most in the Premier League, which could be more challenging for Penders than Martinez.

Filling in for Martinez, Penders punched the ball into his own goal on his first league start for Chelsea in a 2-0 loss to Tottenham Hotspur.

Recent findings suggest that however, he impressed against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup, then Manchester United and Sunderland in the Premier League. He won the Save of the Month award for October for denying Bryan Mbeumo at Stamford Bridge.

Penders won October's Save of the Month award for denying Man United's Bryan Mbeumo.

Industry observers note that penders is clearly a terrific talent, and it would be tempting to continue to show trust in him by having him face Leeds. Chelsea then face Nottingham Forest, Crystal Palace, Liverpool and Manchester City in a rush of fixtures as we head into December.

It is a substantial decision to be made by Alonso, and would take bravery for him to stick with his prodigy in Penders, when we know the experience of the proven Martinez weighs heavy in his mind.

Chelsea vice captain Moises Caicedo is to be checked over at Cobham after a small injury scare while the influential midfielder was away with Ecuador.

According to recent reports, caicedo would be expected to wear the armband at Leeds in Reece James’ ongoing absence. He is set to return to the training ground on Thursday to be assessed.

The 25-year-old played 84 minutes in Ecuador’s first fixture of the break, a 2-0 victory against Costa Rica in which he scored. However, he then asked to be substituted at half-time of their 2-0 win over Bolivia, which ended in the early hours of Wednesday morning. Captaining his country, it was believed to be due to a small physical complaint.

Meanwhile, Chelsea have been looking at the midfield market in the build-up to this January after they missed out on bolstering their options in the summer when Enzo Fernandez was sold to Manchester City. They retain an interest in Bournemouth's Alex Scott.

By Saikat Mandal | 22 Nov 2026 07:39.

Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur are reportedly set to go head-to-head in the race to sign Freiburg forward Igor Matanovic during the January transfer window.

The 23-year-old joined Freiburg in the summer of 2025 and has since made 64 appearances across all competitions for the Bundesliga outfit.

The Croatian enjoyed an impressive campaign last season, registering 15 goals in all competitions, and has already found the net eight times in 2026-27, including five strikes in the Bundesliga.

Man Utd have been linked with a move for Matanovic in recent weeks, although Arsenal and Chelsea are also understood to be monitoring his situation.

According to a fresh report from iNews, Tottenham have now joined the pursuit of Matanovic, with Roberto De Zerbi keen to bolster his attacking options ahead of the second half of the campaign.

Man Utd are also reportedly firmly in the running for the Croatian international, although Freiburg are expected to demand a fee in the region of £50m before sanctioning his departure.

Spurs, meanwhile, could make room for a upcoming centre-forward by offloading Richarlison in January, with the club reportedly prepared to accept an offer of around £10m as Turkish outfit Trabzonspor continue to retain an interest in the Brazilian.

Pochettino would also welcome the arrival of another forward to provide competition and support for Benjamin Sesko, particularly with Joshua Zirkzee potentially heading for the exit after managing just 89 minutes of Premier League action this season.

Although Matanovic is understood to have attracted interest from clubs in other leagues, reports suggest that the Freiburg striker would favour a move to the Premier League should the opportunity arise.

After enduring a nightmare start to the campaign, De Zerbi's side have shown signs of a considerable revival and have climbed to ninth in the Premier League table, giving the Italian some encouragement ahead of the January window.

Strengthening the centre-forward department remains a priority for Spurs, who have also been linked with Bournemouth youngster Eli Junior Kroupi, although they could face stiff competition from Liverpool, Arsenal and Barcelona for his signature.

Endrick is another name who could attract interest from Premier League clubs after struggling to make a significant impression under Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, although any potential move is more likely to materialise in the form of a loan deal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Louis Saha believes Manchester United should have signed Nicolas Jackson before his £65million move from Chelsea to Aston Villa.

Jackson enjoyed a fast start to life at Chelsea, scoring 17 goals in all competitions during his first season at Stamford Bridge.

But the Senegalese striker failed to hit those heights during the 2024-25 campaign and Chelsea sent him on loan to Bayern Munich last season.

The performances of Joao Pedro complicated Jackson’s future upon his return from his loan in Germany, and a sale to Villa was eventually sanctioned, reuniting the 25-year-old with his former Villarreal boss Unai Emery.

Back under Emery’s tutelage, Jackson has returned to his best, with nine goals in 14 appearances so far this season.

And Saha believes United missed a trick by not trying to sign Jackson over the summer, particularly given Benjamin Sesko’s injury woes, which have seen him miss large swathes of this campaign.

‘Nicolas Jackson is a player that I think Man Utd really missed out on because he’s an experienced striker who plays well under pressure,’ Saha told CasinoHawks.

‘Of course, he misses chances sometimes, but his work rate and ability to keep opposing centre-backs busy are vital for team balance.

‘Aston Villa have done really well with those two players, I would’ve loved them at Old Trafford.’.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Saha feels similarly about midfielder Leon Goretzka, who joined Villa on a free transfer from Bayern Munich this summer, with the Frenchman adding: ‘Leon Goretzka was a bargain for Aston Villa.

According to recent reports, ‘There’s a bit of jealousy seeing someone like Goretzka go to Aston Villa while Man Utd lose Casemiro. You definitely need experienced players in that central area.

‘Adapting to the Premier League isn’t always easy, but Villa went for proven quality. It’s frustrating, as those are the types of opportunities Man United should be capitalizing on.’.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Andoni Iraola believes it is too soon to consider Liverpool as potential Premier League title contenders after they thumped 10-man Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Andoni Iraola believes it is too soon to consider Liverpool as potential Premier League title contenders after they thumped 10-man Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

Liverpool were helped by Leny Yoro's eighth-minute sending-off for a last-man foul on Alexander Isak, with the Reds using their numerical advantage to ruthless effect.

Dominik Szoboszlai flashed home the free-kick from Yoro's challenge in the 10th minute before Florian Wirtz superbly turned Rio Ngumoha's cross into the net three minutes later.

Mauricio Pochettino, taking charge of United for the first time, introduced Harry Maguire for Bryan Mbeumo in an enforced change to try and bring some more defensive stability, but Liverpool eventually breached the Red Devils' back line in the second half.

Bradley Barcola's blistering run ended with a pinpoint cross for Ngumoha to tuck home, with Victor Munoz coming off the bench to seal an emphatic win eight minutes from time.

Since the start of the 2021-22 season, Liverpool's four wins by 4+ goals against United are the most any Premier League team has achieved against another in all competitions.

It was a result that moved Liverpool back into the top four and within one point of Manchester City and Brighton, who dropped points to Fulham and Hull City, respectively.

Arsenal are seven points clear of Liverpool after drawing 2-2 with Newcastle United, but Iraola was keen not to get carried away with the euphoria of beating the Reds' rivals.

Sources indicate that "It's still early days. I think we are missing the two substantial games we lost here at home between Arsenal and [Man City]. They are making the difference in the standings," he mentioned.

"This is still so early. This doesn't stop because we have a very difficult game against Club Brugge, and then we have the massive derby.".

4 – Since the start of the 2021-22 season, Liverpool's four wins by 4+ goals against Manchester United are the most any Premier League team has achieved against another. Another. https://t.co/c5BtjVXvlB.

— OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) November 22, 2026.

Pochettino became the first manager in Premier League history to see his team concede twice and receive a red card in the first half of his first match in charge of a club.

Indeed, it was also the quickest Liverpool had gone 2-0 up in a Premier League match against United, going two ahead after just 12 minutes and 40 seconds.

Iraola is now unbeaten in his seven Premier League matches against United (W3 D4), and even quipped that his players could celebrate at half-time after going two goals in front.

"I think it's a significant win; always against United it is a big game," Iraola added. "I think also you can enjoy it; you can see it coming.

Recent findings suggest that "It's difficult to enjoy in the Premier League. Normally you suffer even if you win, but I think we could celebrate at half-time and enjoy it a little bit and have lovely moments.

Industry observers note that "We have missed some clear chances. In other games you will remember those chances; we've controlled the game, and everything was happening around the box.

"It's a 4-0 that was good for us in the standings but also confidence-wise, trying to get better results here at home.".

There was also another standout display from Wirtz, who created 10 chances in open play for Liverpool, the most by a player in a Premier League match since Man City's David Silva against West Brom in March 2015 (11).

Wirtz now has eight goal involvements (three goals, five assists) in 16 appearances across all competitions in 2026-27, with the Liverpool attacker also starring in the international break under former Reds boss Jurgen Klopp with three goals in two games for Germany in the Nations League.

"He's in a lovely moment, and we want to keep him there as much as we can," Iraola said of Wirtz.

"He's in a situation against 10 players where you need players like him to control the situation and see the passes in behind.

"He's also arriving more and not just scoring but being a threat. He's becoming another option, and I'm happy with him.".

#72023. Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 50 min read (9994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section.
  • It has been revealed that the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7.
  • Recent findings suggest that for example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections1,2,3, and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips4. In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model5. The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

It has been revealed that the Landau model provides a powerful framework for understanding many phases of matter through the lens of spontaneous symmetry breaking6,7. In superfluids and superconductors, this breaking manifests in the emergence of a macroscopic condensate that exhibits long-range phase coherence. This coherence is ultimately responsible for properties such as dissipationless transport8,9, the Josephson effect10, and in the case of superconductivity the Meissner effect11. Although relatively robust in bulk systems, in lower-dimensional systems, the enhanced effect of fluctuations—and in particular topological defects—can suppress this long-range phase coherence and govern superfluid transport4,12.

Recent findings suggest that for example, in a voltage-biased superconducting wire, the applied voltage continuously winds the superconducting phase, causing an increase of the phase gradient between the contacts. The supercurrent, proportional to this gradient, would grow without bound unless intermittent phase fluctuations relax the accumulated gradient. By relaxing the gradient, the fluctuations dissipate energy, thereby causing a resistance3,13. The characteristics of the fluctuations and their corresponding resistance depend on the dimensionality of the setup as follows.

In one-dimensional (1D) wires, discrete relaxation events known as phase slips dominate the dynamics. Microscopically, a phase slip occurs when the magnitude of the superconducting order parameter is transiently and locally suppressed over a healing length ξ. Where the amplitude vanishes, the phase is ill-defined, allowing for phase jumps of 2π. As the order parameter recovers, the wire returns to a state with a uniform amplitude but a reduced phase gradient4 (Fig. 1a, top row).

Recent findings suggest that a, Dissipation in a narrow, quasi-1D channel occurs because of phase slips, in which a depletion of the order parameter allows for a relaxation of the phase gradient and kinetic energy (top row). The corresponding phase (colour-coded) evolution of a phase slip in a narrow channel is plotted in the central row. In a wide, quasi-2D channel, dissipation is governed by vortex–antivortex pairs traversing the channel (bottom row). b, A transport channel of programmable width connects two superfluid reservoirs (blue). The channel is formed by two repulsive beams (green and orange), one of which is tunable by a DMD.

According to recent reports, in two-dimensional (2D) geometries, such as thin films, dissipation instead arises from the nucleation and motion of topological defects known as vortices. A vortex is a point-like singularity of the phase around which the phase winds by 2π, with a small core in which the amplitude is suppressed. Driven by a current, vortices move across the film and dissipate energy. Each time a vortex traverses the sample, the phase difference between the contacts relaxes by 2π. Repeated vortex crossings generate a finite voltage and hence an effective resistance14,15 (Fig. 1a, bottom row). In intermediate, thin-strip geometries, both vortex flow and phase slips may contribute to dissipation.

According to recent reports, previous studies included experiments on superconducting rings16; Dayem-bridge nanowires17,18,19,20; Bose–Einstein condensates in dumbbell21,22, cylindrical23 or toroidal geometries24; optical lattices25,26; and fermionic Josephson junctions27,28,29. These previous studies have explored various facets of phase-slip and vortex physics, including direct imaging of vortices28,30,31,32, the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless phase transition33 and the recent observation of Shapiro steps in atomic Josephson junctions34,35. However, the experimental challenge of isolating and characterizing geometric or dimensional effects on dissipation remains unresolved.

With the rise of quantum simulation of devices based on highly controllable ultracold atomic gases36,37, it is now possible to shed fresh light on how these dissipative processes emerge in quantum systems.

Recent findings suggest that in this work, we use ultracold, strongly interacting fermions in a two-terminal configuration to study nonlinear transport through a digitally programmable channel. The optically shaped channel can be reproducibly tuned from a quasi-1D to a quasi-2D geometry, providing a platform ideally suited for probing the influence of geometry on fluctuation-driven dissipation in the absence of defects or impurities.

In the narrow, 1D channel limit, we identify signatures of phase slips, in agreement with the Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin (LAMH) theory4,38,39. In particular, we observe the predicted exponential suppression of the LAMH activation factor over many orders of magnitude on widening the channel. For even larger widths, the system crosses over to a 2D regime in which dissipation is dominated by vortices, as indicated by the observed power-law dependence of the current–voltage characteristics predicted for vortex dynamics.

Beyond establishing these limiting behaviours, our measurements provide a direct window into the crossover between 1D and 2D transport, a regime in which analytical modelling is challenging. It is in this crossover that widening the channel paradoxically increases its resistance. More broadly, our results highlight the utility of ultracold atomic superfluids as a platform for quantum simulation of nonequilibrium transport.

In a recent development, we prepare a balanced mixture of the lowest and third-lowest hyperfine states of fermionic 6Li in the unitary regime. A total of 2N = 2.7 ± 0.1 × 105 atoms are cooled to T/TF = 0.144 ± 0.007, where N denotes the number of atom pairs, TF denotes the Fermi temperature, and the errors in both quantities denote the uncertainties due to shot-to-shot fluctuations. The temperature corresponds to T/TC ≈ 0.7, where TC ≈ 0.2TF denotes the critical temperature40. The atoms are confined in a cigar-shaped, harmonic trap with trapping frequencies (νx, νy, νz) = (222 ± 7, 28.1 ± 0.1, 195 ± 5) Hz.

Industry observers note that as shown in Fig. 1a, a repulsive TEM0,1 beam, propagating in the x-direction, is aligned with the trap centre. It divides the atomic cloud into two reservoirs, separated by a quasi-2D transport region that is 51 ± 1 μm long and provides confinement of ν2D = 10.46 ± 0.09 kHz along z. Within the central 27 ± 0.5 μm of this plane, the atoms are further confined in the x-direction to a channel of variable width w. The channel is defined by a repulsive beam propagating along z, shaped by a digital micromirror device (DMD). It enables reproducible tunability of w from 0.9 ± 0.5 μm to 19.8 ± 0.5 μm, in which the uncertainty is dominated by and calculated from the resolution limit of our projection system (numerical aperture = 0.53, λ = 532 nm). Note that given the dimensions of our setup, we are not in the Josephson regime (see Methods, ‘No Josephson oscillations’). A third, attractive Gaussian beam (not shown) illuminates the transport channel and its connections to the reservoirs, locally increasing the degeneracy. A more detailed description of this effect as well as of the overall setup can be found in ref. 41.

According to recent reports, at time t = 0, we prepare a relative atom-pair imbalance between the two reservoirs, ΔN/N = (Nl − Nr)/(Nl + Nr), where Nl,r denote the number of atom pairs in the left and right reservoirs. An initial imbalance of ΔN/N ≈ 0.1 relaxes through an approximately constant initial current, followed by damped oscillations of the imbalance. The discharge is distinctly non-exponential, indicating a nonlinear response. The damping, and in particular its dependence on the channel width w, carries information about the underlying microscopic mechanisms.

In a recent development, the key data of our measurement series are shown in Fig. 2a. We record transport traces for w between 0.9 ± 0.5 μm and 19.8 ± 0.5 μm. As w increases, the magnitude of the initial current increases, which manifests in a steeper initial slope. Concurrently, both the oscillation frequency and amplitude grow. The frequency rises from just below 10 Hz to approximately 18 Hz (see also Extended Data Fig. 1). For the narrowest channel (w = 0.9 ± 0.5 μm), the oscillation amplitude is comparable to the noise floor and barely resolved. By contrast, for the widest channel (w = 19.8 ± 0.5 μm), the amplitude reaches ΔN/N ≈ 0.06.

It has been revealed that a, Atom transport (imbalance ΔN/N as a function of time t) of a unitary Fermi gas through channels of increasing width shows distinctively changing dissipation characteristics. The data are compared with fitted phase slip (LAMH) and vortex models. The models both describe the TNR in the circuit (b), capturing either phase slips or vortices. The LAMH model fits narrow channels, whereas the vortex model fits wide channels. The measurements for different channel widths are vertically offset for clarity. The statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically four to five measurements per data point) are smaller than the marker size. c, A quality-of-fit \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis substantiates the change of the dominant model apparent in a.

The damping exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on w. At longer transport times (for example, t = 0.3 s), the remaining oscillation amplitude reaches a maximum for intermediate channel widths (see also Fig. 4). These signals suggest distinct dissipative mechanisms in the narrow and wide channel limits, which we analyse quantitatively below.

The general characteristics of the dynamics can be understood as arising from the interplay between the potential energy stored in the reservoirs, the kinetic energy inside the channel and the dissipative processes we want to investigate. To study these dissipative processes, we model our system with an equivalent RLC circuit shown in Fig. 2b. We first characterize the capacitance and inductance of the circuit to subsequently infer the dissipative (resistive) processes by fitting the dynamics of the circuit to the measurements. The capacitances, inductance and resistance in the circuit model correspond to the compressibility of the atomic reservoirs, the inertia of the atoms and the dissipative processes in the channel, respectively. We explore these elements in the following starting with the capacitors. As the model circuit features two capacitors in series, each with a capacitance C, the effective capacitance of the circuit is Ceff = C/2. The compressibility κeff of the gas allows to quantify this equivalent capacitance Ceff (potential energy per atom pair displaced from equilibrium) through \(\frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{\kappa }_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Delta {E}_{\mathrm{pot}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}{(\Delta N/2)}^{2}/{C}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). We measured the compressibility of our sample (Methods, ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) to find hCeff = 15.8 ± 0.5 s, where h is Planck’s constant. Next we quantify the inductance. To do so, we assume all channels have box-like potentials. A charge-neutral atom-pair current I carries a kinetic energy Ekin that depends on w. We define the inductance of our systems using \({E}_{{\rm{kin}}}\equiv \frac{1}{2}L{I}^{2}.\) We developed a model that predicts a functional dependence.

(Methods, ‘Derivation of the inductance’). By analysing the oscillation frequencies observed in our measurements and noting that in a weakly damped circuit, the frequencies are given by \(\omega (w)\approx 1/\sqrt{L(w){C}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\), we find ℓc/h = 3.01 ± 0.03 × 10−5 μm s and Lres/h = 3.06 ± 0.04 × 10−6 s. Although the details are provided in the Supplementary Information, here we state that the first term in equation (1) captures the kinetic energy in the channel, whereas the second term accounts for the kinetic energy in the reservoirs.

Phase slips and vortices dissipate the kinetic energy of the current into heat. So, they effectively act as a topological nonlinear resistor (TNR). With L and C determined, the resistance R remains the sole unknown component in our circuit. Owing to the nature of phase slips, R is topological and nonlinear, meaning it depends not only on the geometry but also on the current.

Showing how R depends on geometry, in particular in relation to the length scale given by ξ ≈ 1.2 μm (Methods, ‘Estimate of ξ’), reveals the nature of the underlying dissipative processes. To do so, we fit the width-dependent resistance R(w) in the equations of motion of an RLC circuit (derived in Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’).

According to recent reports, for narrow, quasi-1D channels (w ≱ 2ξ), we expect the system to be in the phase slip regime. The LAMH model predicts4.

defined using R = V/I, where R0 is the characteristic resistance, w0 is the characteristic width, and I0 = 2kBT/h, where kB is the Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature. The exponential suppression of R with w reflects the thermally activated phase-slip rate scaling with \(\varGamma \propto \exp (-\Delta F/({k}_{{\rm{B}}}T))\) (ref. 18), where the free energy barrier for phase slips is ΔF ∝ w. The sinh(I/I0) term can intuitively be understood as follows: at small |I/I0| ≪ 1, phase slips occur in both directions with roughly equal probability; as the bias increases slightly, phase slips that relax the current become more probable. For large |I/I0| ≫ 1, sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2. reflecting the local destabilization of the superfluid and the resulting exponential increase in the phase-slip probability.

Sources indicate that using our predetermined C and L(w), we determine R0 and w0 by fitting them simultaneously to the measurements of our four narrowest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’). Assuming that the LAMH model can be used to describe our system, a simultaneous fit to multiple channel widths provides a robust extraction of the model parameters but enforces the predicted exponential suppression of RLAMH with w. We find R0/h = 102.3±0.2 and w0 = 49.7(6) nm, where the errors denote the uncertainties of the fit. The resulting fits (shown in Fig. 2a) largely capture the dynamics for channels with a width up to w = 2.5 μm. This is quantified by \(\mathrm{NRMSE}\,=\) \(\sqrt{{\sum }_{i}{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}/N}/({m}_{\max }-{m}_{\min }) < 0.06\), where mi and fi denote the measured and fitted imbalances, respectively, and mmax − mmin is the measured signal range. However, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis \(({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 9)\) shown in Fig. 2c suggests additional systematic effects beyond the very small statistical uncertainties of the measurements (typically on the level of 0.004). These systematic effects could originate from the approximation of modelling the channel with a box-like potential or the attractive beam illuminating the channel locally increasing the temperature. Outside the validity range of the model, the quality of the fits degrades noticeably, failing to capture the phase of the oscillations and underestimating their damping.

Industry observers note that in a second step, we validate the choice of the LAMH model by fitting RLAMH(w) to each curve individually. In contrast to the simultaneous fit, these individual fits do not enforce the predicted scaling RLAMH(w) and therefore provide an independent test of whether the scaling is present in the data. Within the validity regime of the model, the individual fits reproduce the predicted exponential scaling over many orders of magnitude, as shown in Fig. 3a.

Sources indicate that a, The fitted phase-slip resistance RLAMH(w), for narrow channels, reveals the exponential suppression with width, as predicted by LAMH theory. b, The fitted vortex resistivity ρv(w), for wide channels, shows the predicted power law. Inside the crossover region (2–4ξ), that is, outside the validity range of the models, both scalings break down (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’). Note that a and b display different quantities (resistance compared with resistivity) characterizing different regimes (1D compared with 2D) and are therefore not intended to be compared across the dimensional crossover. The error bars represent the error of the fit.

In a recent development, this is the first main finding of this paper. Compared with RLAMH(w), the total resistance R(I, w) apparent in the measurements (Fig. 2a) varies much less. As we initialize a fixed potential bias in our system, the exponential geometric suppression (R ∝ exp(−w/w0)) approximately cancels the current-induced exponential enhancement (R ∝ sinh(I/I0) ≈ exp(I/I0)/2). This allows RLAMH to be inferred over a wide range—more than 10 decades—while only exploring a relatively modest dynamic range of R. Importantly, the observed scaling of RLAMH(w) is contained within the data itself and is not just an artefact of the choice of the model. This becomes evident when the model is applied outside its validity regime, where the scaling breaks down immediately (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’).

In quasi-2D channels (w ≳ 4ξ), phase slips become energetically unfavourable, as their activation energy increases exponentially with w. Instead, dissipation is expected to be governed by vortex flow. Owing to the vortices, we expect to see a power-law dependence in the pair-current density J:.

According to recent reports, where J0 = I0/ξ. A derivation, building on the results of ref. 5, is provided in the Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’. By fitting α and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) simultaneously to the data of our four widest channels (Methods, ‘RLC circuit modelling and fitting’), we find \(\alpha =1.98\pm 0.04,{\mathop{R}\limits^{ \sim }}_{0}/h=1{0}^{-4.79\pm 0.07}\). As apparent from Fig. 2a, this model captures the dynamics for channels in the 2D regime (NRMSE ≱ 0.06). In these cases, \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\lesssim 4\). Note that the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, and for wide channels, the box-potential approximation is safer compared with narrow channels. Apart from these statistical tests, we validate our model by fixing α to its global fit value but fitting ρv to each individual curve. Within the validity range of the model, these individual fits agree with the predicted power-law ρv ∝ wα−1 (Fig. 3b). This scaling is the second main finding of the paper. The scaling breaks down outside the validity regime of the model (Methods, ‘Breakdown of scaling laws’), providing evidence that the observed scaling is a feature of the data, not a mere artefact of the enforced power law R ∝ Jα−1. When approaching the dimensional crossover w ≱ 4ξ, while still largely capturing the dynamics, the model begins to slightly but systematically underestimate the amplitude of the oscillations at long times. Presumably, because the approximation of sufficiently large w used in the derivation of R(J) ceases to hold (Methods, ‘Vortices in a finite width’). The eventual breakdown of the vortex model at w ≈ 4ξ marks the end of the 2D regime: the vortex model should be valid only when vortex–antivortex pairs are available as excitations. As each vortex has a radius of ξ, such an excitation requires w ≳ 4ξ. This leaves a gap between the validity ranges of the phase slip and the vortex model, in which neither model provides a microscopically satisfactory description. In this gap, there is a dimensional crossover, in which both phase slips and vortices compete.

The underdamped oscillations allow us to characterize dissipation in our system using only a few basic assumptions, while staying agnostic to the dissipation mechanism. This is particularly useful to analyse the dimensional crossover, in which neither the phase-slip nor the vortex model provide a satisfactory microscopical description. We split the total energy Etot into a potential (capacitive) energy EC and a kinetic (inductive) energy EL. We assume Etot = EC(ΔN) + EL(I, w) with EC ∝ ΔN2 and EL(I = 0, w) = 0. For each channel width w, we extract the times ti,w at which ΔN(t = ti, w) reaches an extremum and thus I ≈ 0. There, the system has minimal inductive energy (EL ≈ 0) and maximal capacitive energy. The fraction of the initial energy remaining in the system is then given by.

Sources indicate that the remaining energy as a function of time and channel width is shown in Fig. 4. The plot is obtained by cubic interpolation between the measured points, performed linearly in time and logarithmically in width.

Recent findings suggest that the remaining energy in the oscillator paradoxically varies non-monotonically as a function of the channel width w. For a given time after the initial decay, the maximum appears in the crossover region, near w = 4 μm ≈ 3ξ, in which phase slips and vortices are suppressed but competing. The crosses mark the measurement points (typically four to five measurements per cross) between which we interpolate. We estimate the individual data points to have a typical positive bias of 0.5% and a statistical uncertainty smaller than 2% (Methods, ‘Error estimation’).

For a fixed width, the energy decays over time, reflecting dissipation. At any given time t > 0.15 s, Et(w)/E0 varies non-monotonically with the channel width, exhibiting a clear maximum near w ≈ 3ξ, corresponding to a minimal effective resistance. We call this deviation from the expected monotonicity the ‘quantum resistance paradox’ and consider it the third and last main finding of this paper. Note that the activation energy for phase slips increases exponentially with channel width, whereas vortex–antivortex pairs require sufficiently wide channels to form. The observed non-monotonicity thus suggests a transition in the underlying dissipation mechanism and a crossover from 1D to 2D physics.

Sources indicate that we have investigated atom transport between two bulk superfluids through channels across different dimensional regimes and observed distinct behaviours. In narrow, quasi-1D channels, our data are in agreement with those of the LAMH model. We infer the geometric suppression of the phase slips by many orders of magnitude, providing the first experimental confirmation of the predicted geometric scaling. For wide, quasi-2D channels, dissipation is captured by a vortex flow model. The borders of the 1D and 2D regimes appear close to the theoretically expected length scale. A measurement of energy decay, agnostic to microscopic details, provides further evidence for a transition in the dissipation mechanism for channels of intermediate width, which paradoxically exhibit the least energy loss. These findings not only suggest routes for optimizing energy transport in mesoscopic devices but also provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts to describe the delicate phase-slip and vortex-flow mechanisms in the dimensional crossover in superfluids and superconductors42,43,44.

Our setup is analogous to an RLC circuit with the mapping presented in Extended Data Table 1.

The procedures for determining the capacitance C and the inductance L are described in sections ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’ and ‘Derivation of the inductance’. Here, we derive the governing equations and provide additional details on the fitting procedure used to determine R, as presented in the main text.

The total number of atoms in each reservoir is measured directly using absorption images of both hyperfine states (|1⟩ and |3⟩), taken in rapid succession. To determine the total number of pairs in each reservoir Nl,r, we use both measurements, as this reduces statistical uncertainty. Specifically, \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}}}=({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|1\rangle }+{N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|3\rangle })/2\), where \({N}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{r}};|i\rangle }\) denotes the number of atoms in the left and right reservoirs in state |i⟩. However, the second image (state |3⟩) shows a cloud that has absorbed some energy from the first imaging pulse and is therefore slightly distorted. To avoid systematic effects from this distortion on C and T, we use only the image of the lowest hyperfine state (|1⟩) to extract the compressibility and temperature of the cloud, assuming these are identical for both states. We verified that our preparation is equivalent for both states by inverting the imaging sequence. We describe our system in terms of pairs and report C, L and R for pairs and pair currents, respectively.

As shown in Fig. 2b, our RLC circuit consists of two capacitors (reservoirs) in series. We replace these two capacitors C by an effective capacitance Ceff = C/2. With this replacement, we obtain a standard RLC series circuit with an initially charged capacitor but no externally applied voltage.

Applying Kirchhoff’s voltage law and charge conservation, we find.

Using the mapping Q ↔ ΔN/2 and Ceff = C/2, we obtain.

In a recent development, phase slips and vortices induce nonlinear resistances, so R = R(I) or R = R(J), where I and J denote the pair current and pair-current density, respectively. Depending on the model, we use.

Equations (9) and (10) are then integrated numerically.

It has been revealed that experimentally, transport is initiated by ramping down a blue-detuned beam that blocks the channel. A sudden quench of this beam slightly perturbs the reservoirs, so we instead ramp it down over 10 ms. This introduces an unknown initial condition I(t = 0). For each curve, we fit I(t = 0) ∈ [0, Iavg], where Iavg is the average current during the initial decay (before oscillations). To avoid giving undue weight to the first measured point, we fit ΔNfit(t = 0) ∈ [0.8, 1.2] ⋅ ΔNmeasured(t = 0). These bounds are necessary to prevent the models from ignoring the initial decay outside their validity regime. In particular, this is the case for the LAMH model when fitting data of wide channels, where only a few points represent the initial dynamics.

For numerical stability, R0 and \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\) are fitted on a logarithmic scale, whereas α and w0 are fitted linearly.

Finally, we discuss the fitting weights. Each configuration (t, w) has five measurements. Points with preparation errors (low atom number) are excluded, typically leaving four to five measurements per point and occasionally three. The experimental standard deviation is calculated for each configuration individually. We assume that for a given w, the uncertainty is independent of t. To prevent the fit from being dominated by points with unrealistically small uncertainties, both the fitting and the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) calculations replace individual error bars with the median error bar of all the data sharing w.

According to recent reports, the \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) analysis shown in Fig. 2c is performed as follows. The uncertainty of the measured points is assumed to be identical for all points belonging to a specific channel width. For each channel width, the model is fitted, either with 2.5 effective degrees of freedom (R0, w0, ΔN0, I0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0},\alpha ,\Delta {N}_{0},{I}_{0}\)), where the first two parameters are shared among four channels (2/4 = 0.5) if the channel participates in the global fit of the respective model, or two degrees of freedom (ΔN0, I0) otherwise. The reduced chi-squared is then calculated using \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}=\frac{1}{n-m}\sum \frac{{({m}_{i}-{f}_{i})}^{2}}{{\sigma }^{2}}\), where mi are the measured values, fi the corresponding values fitted by the model, σ the uncertainty shared by all measurement points of a specific width, n the number of measured points and m = 2.5 or m = 2 the number of effectively fitted degrees of freedom.

According to recent reports, we discuss how the fitted models are affected by the various sources of systematic uncertainty. Specifically, we investigate how systematic uncertainties in the capacitance C, the channel width w and the temperature T affect the quality of the model fits and the inferred parameters RLAMH and α.

It has been revealed that assume that the true physical capacitance \(\widetilde{C}\) differs from the calculated value (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’) by a factor γ, such that \(C=\gamma \widetilde{C}\). In our analysis, the effective inductance L is determined (see section ‘Derivation of the inductance’) before fitting the resistance by analysing the underdamped, multi-period oscillations of the system. Owing to the observation of multiple periods, the frequency can be measured with good accuracy and precision. A systematic shift γ ≠ 1 would therefore result in an inverse scaling of the extracted inductance curve, \(L\approx \widetilde{L}/\gamma \), where \(\widetilde{L}\) represents the true physical inductance. Inspecting the underlying equation of motion of the circuit (equation (2)) demonstrates that the extracted resistance scales identically with this factor (R ∝ 1/γ). This uniform rescaling by 1/α can be absorbed in the prefactor R0 or \({\widetilde{R}}_{0}\), leaving the quality of the fits, scalings, the inferred dynamic ranges and the geometric suppression constant w0 entirely unaffected.

According to recent reports, the geometric potential landscape is projected onto the atoms using a DMD. Although physical pixel spacing and optical demagnification ratio are known accurately, the primary source of spatial uncertainty stems from the finite resolution of the imaging optics. The finite resolution effectively blurs the repulsive potential walls of the channel. Consequently, having to choose where to define the sharp boundaries of the model (spaced by w) within this blurred profile introduces a systematic uncertainty Δw.

Importantly, this geometric uncertainty of roughly 0.5 μm is expected to be shared across all channel configurations and does not affect each channel independently of the others. For channels in the 1D regime, the initial discharge through the narrowest channels is characterized by an extended period of nearly constant current in which inertial forces are negligible (∣L dI/dt∣ ≪ |RI|). In this regime, the system behaves predominantly as a nonlinear RC circuit, approximately decoupling the resistance fit from the precise value of L. Then, a uniform translation of w by Δw alters the resistances by a constant factor. For the LAMH model, \(R(w+\Delta w)\propto \exp (-\Delta w/{w}_{0})\). Similarly to the capacitance error, this effect is entirely absorbed by a re-normalization of the global prefactor R0, preserving both the dynamic range of RLAMH and its slope set by w0. The relatively high value of \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) for the LAMH model might be caused by the experiment that violates the assumption of box-like channel potentials. For the channels in the 2D regime, Δw/w ≪ 1, so we expect systematic effects caused by Δw ≠ 0 to be small and the approximation of modelling the channels as box-like to be safe.

It has been revealed that although we calibrated our measurements with the thermodynamic reference point of Bose–Einstein condensation, our measured atom-pair numbers and temperatures (see sections ‘High-saturation imaging’ and ‘Thermodynamic state extraction by 2D equation of state fitting’) might be subject to systematic errors. An error in the inferred pair-number \(N=\gamma \widetilde{N}\), where N is the inferred particle number and \(\widetilde{N}\) is the physical particle number, would force a corresponding shift in C, thereby rescaling L and R as discussed above. Moreover, it would rescale I. As the current enters the expression for the resistance in the vortex model only in the form of a power law, it would merely shift \(\widetilde{R}\) by a constant factor γ−α. Again, this constant factor would affect neither α, nor the quality of the vortex-model fits, nor the quality of its scaling law. As the vortex model does not contain an explicit temperature dependence, it is unaffected by potential systematic effects in T. For the LAMH model, the situation is different. The temperature enters the model explicitly through I0 = 2kBT/h. Variations in both N and T ultimately tie into the ratio I/I0. Because this ratio controls the degree of nonlinearity of the circuit, we can model their combined systematic impact by analysing variations in I0 alone.

The initial discharge of the narrowest channels is distinctly nonlinear (implying I ≫ I0), whereas the subsequent oscillations are approximately sinusoidal (implying I ≱ I0). Consequently, the ratio I/I0 is constrained by the geometric profile of the relaxation curves. However, systematic effects that affect the ratio I/I0 do also affect the quality of fit and the dynamic range of RLAMH. In general, if I/I0 is lowered (by decreasing I or increasing T), the circuit is less nonlinear and the dynamic range of RLAMH decreases, whereas an increase in the ratio has the opposite effect. Although the parameter I0 is constrained in the LAMH model, we performed additional fittings, where I0 was a global fit parameter, to effectively account for potential systematic errors in I or T. The best fits are achieved with I0,fit = 3.50(1)I0, reducing \({\chi }_{\nu }^{2}\) averaged over the five narrowest channels, by more than a factor of 2. A possible cause for this could be that the attractive Gaussian beam illuminating the channel locally heats the channel, thereby increasing I0. Note that this beam also increases the local degeneracy such that we would still expect the channel to be deeply degenerate. Although in the case of fitted I0, the dynamic range of RLAMH is reduced, it continues to span more than four orders of magnitude. The values are still in good agreement with the predicted exponential scaling.

For all channel widths except the narrowest one, we observe underdamped, long-lived oscillations. As these oscillations remain underdamped, the influence of the nonlinear resistance on the oscillation frequency is expected to be small. To extract the inductance of the channel for each width (except the narrowest one), we exclude the initial transient dynamics up to the first, global minimum occurring at a time t = t1,w. The remaining data are fitted with a damped sinusoidal function \({f}_{w}(t)={A}_{w}\exp (-(t-{t}_{1,w})/{\tau }_{w})\sin ({\omega }_{w}t+{\phi }_{{\rm{w}}})+\Delta {N}_{w,\mathrm{offset}},\) where Aw, τw, ωw, ϕw, and ΔNw,offset are fitting parameters. Small offsets |ΔNw,offset| < 0.018 account for potential alignment errors that cause the oscillations to centre around slightly nonzero values. Using the inferred effective capacitance Ceff of our circuit (see section ‘Derivation of the reservoir capacitance’), we determine the total inductance for a given channel width as \({L}_{w}=1/(({\omega }_{w}^{2}+{\tau }_{w}^{-2}){C}_{\mathrm{eff}})\approx 1/({\omega }_{w}^{2}C),\) where the approximation is equivalent to the result for an undamped LC circuit and holds for weakly damped circuits. Although the quantitative difference in our case is minute, we do include the τ-term capturing the effect of the resistance lowering the oscillation frequency of the RLC circuit. Note that for the wide channels in particular, fitting a damped sine to the oscillatory data is a pragmatic choice that allows for an approximation of the inductance, the signature of which is primarily contained in the frequency of the oscillation. Over extended periods of time, however, the damped sine and the dynamics of the vortex model would appear different, as the latter does not feature an exponentially decaying amplitude. This kinetic inductance Lw quantifies the kinetic energy associated with a given pair current I. Although the main contribution arises from the transport channel itself, there is also a residual contribution because of particle motion in the adjoining 2D and 3D regions, whose geometries are independent of the channel width. We therefore write \(L(w)={L}_{\mathrm{channel}}(w)+{L}_{\mathrm{res}}\). Assuming a constant particle density inside the channel, the mass of particles in the transport channel (M) scales with its width, M ∝ w. For a given current, the corresponding particle velocity in the channel thus scales inversely, \({v}_{\mathrm{channel}}\propto \frac{1}{w}\). Consequently, the kinetic energy associated with a fixed I scales as \({E}_{\mathrm{kin}}=M{v}_{\mathrm{channel}}^{2}/2\propto w{(1/w)}^{2}=1/w\), implying that Lchannel(w) ∝ 1/w. We therefore model the total inductance as.
